A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system of computers spread across many cities that store copies of websites so pages load quickly no matter where a visitor sits. Every website normally lives on one machine called the origin server, the original computer holding the real, complete version of a site. If everyone worldwide had to fetch data from that single machine, people far away would wait a long time for pages to appear. A CDN solves this by placing copies of the site on servers positioned near visitors, called edge locations because they sit at the edge of the network, close to where people actually are. When someone requests a page, the nearby edge location checks whether it already has a saved copy; finding one is called a cache hit, meaning the answer can be delivered instantly without contacting the distant origin server at all. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries that each keep popular books in stock, so readers do not need to travel to one faraway central library every time. Only when an edge location lacks a copy does it fetch fresh material from the origin server, then store it for next time. This arrangement keeps websites fast, reduces strain on the original server, and helps pages stay reachable even during heavy traffic.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing the real website | It's the ultimate source that edge locations copy from |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding a copy of site content | It shortens the distance data must travel |
| Cache hit | When a nearby copy answers a request instantly | It speeds up loading and avoids unnecessary trips |
| Latency | The delay between requesting and receiving content | Fewer delays mean smoother, faster browsing |
